config.title: Build mock server for third party dependencies

intro.title: Build mock server for third party dependencies
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a simple mock server using Node.js to simulate third-party API dependencies, allowing you to test your applications without relying on external services. You'll learn how to create an HTTP server that responds to requests with predefined data, mimicking real API behavior. The core concepts include using Node.js's built-in 'http' module to handle requests and responses, and structuring mock endpoints. By the end, you'll have a functional mock server that returns JSON data, helping you develop and test independently.
intro.usecase: Mock servers are essential when developing applications that depend on external APIs or services that are unreliable, rate-limited, or still in development. For example, when building a payment processing dashboard that integrates with Stripe or PayPal, developers can create mock endpoints to simulate transaction responses without hitting production APIs. This allows frontend teams to build UI components like transaction tables and payment status panels while backend services are being developed. Similarly, e-commerce platforms use mock servers to simulate inventory management APIs, enabling developers to test product listing pages and shopping cart functionality independently. This pattern ensures development can continue smoothly even when third-party dependencies are unavailable or unstable.

objectives: Initialize a mock server using a Node.js framework
Configure mock endpoints to simulate third-party API responses
Implement request handlers for different HTTP methods
Manipulate response data to match expected third-party formats
Integrate the mock server with existing application code
Control server behavior through environment variables
Construct dynamic mock responses based on request parameters

steps.title: Import Express and create a basic server
steps.instruction: Import Express using require() and create a basic Express server instance.
steps.hint: Use require('express') to import Express and assign it to a variable, then call express() to create an app instance.
steps.seedCode: // Import Express and create a basic Express server instance
steps.expectedOutcome: You'll have an Express app instance ready to configure.
successCriteria: Express is imported using require() and an Express app instance is created.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're importing Express and creating the app instance.
steps.feedbackWrong: Check the syntax for importing modules and creating Express instances.

steps.title: Initialize the Express app and define port
steps.instruction: Initialize the Express app by calling the Express function and store it in a constant named 'app'. Then, define a constant named 'PORT' with the value 3000.
steps.hint: Use const app = express() to create the Express application instance. Use const PORT = 3000 to define the port number.
steps.expectedOutcome: You should have an Express app instance stored in 'app' and a port constant 'PORT' set to 3000.
successCriteria: The Express app is initialized with express() and stored in a constant named 'app'. A constant named 'PORT' is defined with value 3000.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure you've both initialized the Express app with express() and defined the PORT constant with value 3000.
steps.feedbackWrong: initialize the Express app and define a port constant. Check the hint for guidance.

steps.title: Add middleware for JSON parsing
steps.instruction: Add Express JSON middleware to parse incoming JSON request bodies by calling app.use() with express.json().
steps.hint: Use app.use(express.json()) to add the built-in Express JSON parsing middleware.
steps.expectedOutcome: The server will be able to parse JSON data from incoming POST/PUT requests.
successCriteria: The app.use(express.json()) middleware is added to the Express app.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're using app.use() with express.json() as the argument.
steps.feedbackWrong: The middleware wasn't added correctly. Try using app.use(express.json()) to enable JSON parsing.

steps.title: Create a mock data object
steps.instruction: Create a mock data object named 'mockUsers' containing sample user information to simulate third-party API responses. Place it after the middleware setup.
steps.hint: Define a constant variable called 'mockUsers' and assign it an array of objects. Each object should represent a user with properties like 'id', 'name', and 'email'.
steps.expectedOutcome: A mock data object named 'mockUsers' is created with sample user data, ready to be used in API routes.
successCriteria: A constant named 'mockUsers' is defined as an array containing at least one user object with properties like 'id', 'name', and 'email'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but ensure 'mockUsers' is an array of objects with user properties like 'id', 'name', and 'email'.
steps.feedbackWrong: The mock data object wasn't created correctly. Make sure to define a constant named 'mockUsers' with sample user data.

steps.title: Define a GET endpoint for users
steps.instruction: Define a GET route at '/users' that returns the mock user data as JSON.
steps.hint: Use app.get() to define the route. Inside the route handler, use res.json() to send the mock data as a JSON response.
steps.expectedOutcome: A GET route '/users' is defined that responds with the mock user data in JSON format.
successCriteria: The code includes app.get('/users', ...) that uses res.json(users) to return the mock data.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're using app.get() with '/users' and res.json(users) to send the data.
steps.feedbackWrong: The GET endpoint isn't defined correctly. Check the route path and how you send the JSON response.

steps.title: Add a POST endpoint for creating users
steps.instruction: Create a POST route at '/users' that accepts JSON user data in the request body, adds it to the users array with a new ID, and returns a success response with the created user.
steps.hint: Use app.post() to define the route. Access the request body with req.body. Generate a new ID by finding the maximum existing ID and adding 1. Push the new user to the users array and respond with a 201 status and the created user.
steps.expectedOutcome: A POST endpoint is created that successfully accepts user data, adds it to the mock data, and returns the created user with a 201 status.
successCriteria: A POST route at '/users' is defined using app.post(), it reads req.body, generates a new ID, pushes to the users array, and returns a 201 response with the created user.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure your POST endpoint: 1) Uses app.post('/users', ...), 2) Reads req.body, 3) Generates a new ID, 4) Pushes to users array, 5) Returns status 201 with the created user.
steps.feedbackWrong: The POST endpoint isn't working as expected. Check that you're using app.post() with the correct route, accessing req.body, generating a new ID, updating the users array, and returning the proper response.

steps.title: Implement a PUT endpoint for updating users
steps.instruction: Define a PUT route at '/users/:id' that simulates updating user information. Use req.params.id to find the user and req.body to get the updated data.
steps.hint: Use app.put() with the route path '/users/:id'. Inside, find the user by id from the users array and update their properties with the data from req.body.
steps.expectedOutcome: A PUT endpoint is added that can update user data by ID, returning the updated user or a 404 error if not found.
successCriteria: The PUT route '/users/:id' is defined with app.put(), finds the user by id, updates their data with req.body, and returns appropriate JSON responses.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure your PUT endpoint correctly handles finding the user by ID and updating with the request body data.
steps.feedbackWrong: The PUT endpoint isn't quite right. Remember to use app.put() with '/users/:id', find the user by id from the users array, update their properties, and return appropriate JSON responses.

steps.title: Add a DELETE endpoint for removing users
steps.instruction: Create a DELETE route at '/users/:id' that removes a user from the mock data array based on the provided ID parameter.
steps.hint: Use app.delete() with the route path. Access the ID from req.params, find the user index, and use splice() to remove it from the array.
steps.expectedOutcome: A DELETE endpoint is implemented that removes a user by ID from the users array and returns appropriate HTTP status codes.
successCriteria: The DELETE route is defined with app.delete(), correctly accesses req.params.id, finds the user index, removes the user with splice(), and returns 204 on success or 404 if not found.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure your DELETE route handles finding the user by ID, removes it from the array, and returns the correct status codes.
steps.feedbackWrong: The DELETE endpoint is not properly implemented. Check that you're using app.delete() with the correct route path, accessing the ID parameter, and handling both success and error cases.

steps.title: Start the server and listen on the port
steps.instruction: Start the Express server by calling the listen method on the app object, using the PORT constant.
steps.hint: Use app.listen(PORT, ...) to start the server. You can add a callback function to log a message when the server starts.
steps.expectedOutcome: The server will be operational and ready to handle requests on the defined port.
successCriteria: The app.listen method is called with PORT and a callback function that logs a startup message.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've started the server, but make sure to include a callback function that logs a message for confirmation.
steps.feedbackWrong: The server is not properly started. Check that you're calling app.listen with the correct port and a callback.

steps.title: Add console log for server status
steps.instruction: Update the console.log message inside the app.listen callback to include the server's URL, making it more informative for users.
steps.hint: Modify the existing console.log statement to show the full URL where the server is accessible.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example: Enhanced server status message
console.log(`Server is running at http://localhost:${PORT}`);
steps.expectedOutcome: The server startup message now clearly shows the full URL where the mock server is accessible, providing better feedback for developers.
successCriteria: The console.log statement inside app.listen shows a URL format including 'http://localhost:' and the PORT variable.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've updated the console message, but it should include the full URL format with 'http://localhost:' before the port number.
steps.feedbackWrong: The console message still shows the basic format. Update it to include the full URL like 'http://localhost:${PORT}'.
